where: Section 3 (Power source), quiescent-current paragraph, and Exam trap 3
problem: The numbers contradict the stated claim. A 5 µA quiescent current added to a 10 µA sleep load gives 15 µA total, so the cell lasts 10/15 = 67% of the expected life — a cut of one third, not 'halves battery life'. Exam trap 3 says the regulator 'can double the sleep budget', which would need 10 µA of quiescent current, not 5 µA.
fix: A 5 µA quiescent current against a 10 µA sleep load raises the sleep drain to 15 µA and cuts battery life to two-thirds. In general, sleep life scales as I_sleep ÷ (I_sleep + I_q); halving needs I_q equal to the sleep load (10 µA against 10 µA).

problem: Life is not 'linear in average current'. It is inversely proportional, which is why a ten-times fall in current gives a ten-times rise in life. The wording teaches the wrong relation.
fix: Check the ratio: the current fell ten times and the life rose ten times, because life is inversely proportional to average current (t ∝ 1 ÷ I_avg).

problem: 'Runs no operating system' is too strong: many MCU products run a small real-time operating system such as FreeRTOS. What distinguishes an MCU is that it does not run a full Linux-class OS.
fix: A microcontroller (MCU) puts a CPU, flash memory, RAM and peripherals on one chip and runs bare-metal code or a small real-time OS, not Linux.

problem: The figure note gives LoRa as '2–15 km, 50 kbps', which is only the top of the range; the table in Section 2 says 0.3–50 kbps. Also NB-IoT (about 100 kbps) is drawn at the same vertical level as ZigBee (250 kbps), which breaks the data-rate ordering the axis claims.
fix: LoRa note: '2–15 km, 0.3–50 kbps'. Place NB-IoT just below ZigBee (lower y than ZigBee) so the vertical axis stays ordered by data rate.
